# Solution design — architecture and decisions draft (T001)

**Status:** Working design for later contract authoring, not an implementation, approved production architecture, or `docs/sdlc/solution_design` deliverable. Only the sign-in screen is observed; recovery screens S2–S6 are proposals. No application, tests, or deployment are claimed.

## Proposed architecture and interfaces

One local Flask application, without an external API, queue, provider, database, or outbound mail:

1. **Flask routes and server templates** render S1 and the proposed S2–S6 flow. Jinja templates escape dynamic text; persistent labels, password-type controls, keyboard/focus order, errors, and status announcements are planned. S1 preserves the pictured wording and visual affordances (`REQ-001`–`REQ-006`); the password input's actual masking is a design implementation of `REQ-003`, not a wireframe observation. Do not claim the pictured Sign in button authenticates; its submit outcome needs a decision before a sign-in route is promised.
2. **Recovery service** coordinates account lookup, uniform responses, rate accounting, token issuance/validation, successful reset, session invalidation, and notification append. It returns sanitized outcomes, never account existence or raw tokens to a public template. Password hashing and token generation have narrow injectable adapters. All state-changing decisions are serialized for this small single-process demo.
3. **Application-local store** owns synthetic accounts and password hashes, accepted-request timestamps, reset-token digests and issuance/consumption state, active authenticated session records, short-lived reset intents, and a separate in-memory notification list. The store and recovery service share one lock/transaction boundary; no durable storage or customer data.
4. **Session service** maintains opaque server-side session IDs linked to synthetic account IDs and checks active status for each authenticated request. Reset invalidates *all* represented active sessions for the owner, not only the requester or current browser. A pytest-only fixture may create and exercise multiple sessions without asserting a publicly specified sign-in behavior; no test-only route exposed in the application. If authentication is later approved, it must issue sessions through this service and check them on every protected request, not rely on unrevocable client-only signed cookies.
5. **In-memory sink** records request-link events for known accounts and owner-addressed successful-reset notices. It is an observation point for synthetic tests/operators, not an email transport or public link-discovery endpoint. Never return link secrets on public request/confirmation pages. Whether/how an actual owner receives a link remains unresolved.

Proposed browser contracts (routes and wording are **design choices**, not evidence):

| Browser interaction | Inputs and behavior | Public output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /sign-in` (S1) | None. | Server-rendered wireframe-aligned sign-in card and `GET /reset/request` link. No inferred sign-in result. |
| `GET /reset/request` (S2) | None. | Server-rendered labeled identifier form and S1 return link. |
| `POST /reset/request` | Form: `identifier`, CSRF token. Normalize identifier consistently for lookup; reject malformed/missing input consistently without account-specific hints. Known account: under lock, reserve at most five accepted requests in any trailing one-hour window, issue token, append a reset-link record to sink. Unknown or capped account: do not issue token. | For syntactically valid submissions, return the *same* redirect/status, headers, cookie behavior, and generic S3 page for known, unknown, and capped identifiers. No account existence, count, link, or throttle details. Invalid input or CSRF failures may have generic validation/security errors independent of account lookup. |
| `GET /reset/confirmation` (S3) | None. | Server-rendered generic acknowledgement. Never embed the identifier or token. |
| `GET /reset/<opaque-token>` | Secret URL token. Compute digest and check token unused and `now < issued_at + 30 minutes`; do not consume yet. On success, create an unguessable, server-held short-lived reset intent bound to the token digest and redirect to clean `GET /reset/new`; otherwise redirect to S6. | No secret in rendered HTML, response body, redirect target, error details, or metrics. Do not claim a GET completes a reset. |
| `GET /reset/new` (S4) | Reset-intent cookie; recheck intent and link before displaying form. | Labeled password-type input and CSRF-protected submission form, or S6 when invalid. No inferred password-complexity policy. |
| `POST /reset/complete` | New nonempty password, reset intent, CSRF token. Under the same lock recheck token unused and strictly younger than 30 minutes, hash password, change account hash, mark token consumed, invalidate every represented session, remove intent, and record owner notice after the state change as one all-or-nothing logical operation. | Redirect to S5 only after all required effects succeed; otherwise a generic recoverable error or S6 for unusable link. Never echo password, secret, or account existence. |
| `GET /reset/success` (S5); `GET /reset/unavailable` (S6) | None. | S5 only after success, with return link; S6 shared for invalid, expired, or used links, with new-request and return links. A direct unauthenticated GET of S5 must not be proof that a reset happened. |

For the request route, “accepted” is the internal issuance/reservation event, **not** the externally identical acknowledgement. A per-known-account sliding window discards timestamps `<= now - 1 hour` and accepts only when fewer than five remain. Because internal acceptance differs but public results do not, unknown-account accounting is unnecessary to satisfy the per-*account* limit; do not invent a separate threshold for unknown identifiers. Constant public shape does not guarantee equal wall-clock timing: perform comparable work or pad cautiously, test statistical behavior where practical, and document residual timing risk rather than falsely claiming constant-time web responses. Request-link sink entries remain private, with no public inspection endpoint. An attacker-triggered request to a real account can create a private sink entry; this is not an account-disclosure response.

## Data, security, failure handling, and test seams

- Proposed `Account(id, normalized_identifier, password_hash, synthetic_owner)`, `ResetToken(token_digest, account_id, issued_at_utc, consumed_at_utc?)`, `AcceptedRequest(account_id, accepted_at_utc)`, `ActiveSession(session_id_digest, account_id, active)`, `ResetIntent(intent_digest, token_digest, expires_at_utc)`, and `Notification(account_id/owner, kind, created_at_utc, private_payload)` are application-local conceptual records. No raw passwords or raw reset tokens are persisted in account/token records. Notification link payloads containing raw tokens must be confined to the private in-memory sink, excluded from logs and public responses. Seed only explicitly synthetic `.test` identities; no real identities or external recipients.
- Generate reset secrets with a cryptographically secure RNG; store a one-way digest, use a fresh token per accepted request, and require both an unused state and strict `now < issued_at + 30 minutes` at completion (including a second check after S4 was loaded). Hash new passwords with a maintained adaptive password hash implementation (algorithm/parameters to be selected and documented at implementation); never store plaintext. No password-complexity claim is made. Compare sensitive digest values safely where relevant. CSRF tokens on all state-changing browser forms, session/reset-intent cookies marked HttpOnly, SameSite and Secure where HTTPS is in use; redirect from raw-token URL to clean form, set `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, omit third-party assets, and suppress request paths/query strings in access logs. Initial URL may remain in browser history or sink: document this residual exposure. Demo HTTP/local operation and cookie configuration require explicit documentation; no production HTTPS/deployment configuration is provided.
- In-memory updates are serialized with a process-local lock. Prepare password hash outside lock if needed, then atomically check eligibility and apply password change, token consumption, session invalidation and notification append under the lock; a sink failure must not leave a reported successful reset without its notice. Use a small unit-of-work copy/rollback or failure-free guarded append so every failing branch preserves the pre-reset state, except that a failed attempt may leave non-sensitive diagnostic counters. Duplicate concurrent completions: exactly one may succeed and record one notice. An issuance error must not consume one of the five slots without a corresponding issued token and private sink record. The store is not safe for multiple workers or restarts; do not imply durability or distributed atomicity.
- Injectable UTC clock (timezone-aware), cryptographic token factory, password hasher, sink and fresh store instance allow deterministic pytest cases for fourth/fifth/sixth request, trailing-hour boundary, expiry immediately before/at/after 30 minutes, replay and concurrent completion, synthetic fixture password replacement, multiple active sessions, correct owner notification and sink failure rollback. Flask test client inspects full public response parity (status, redirect, headers, cookies, rendered S3) for otherwise equivalent known/unknown/capped requests, plus wireframe labels/link, server-rendered S2–S6, CSRF and secret-free responses. Test seams must not be public routes. These are future checks, not existing passing tests (`REQ-018`).
- Log aggregate route result categories (`request_received`, `reset_completed`, `invalid_link`, `internal_error`) and safe correlation IDs, never identifiers, secrets, passwords, rendered form contents or private notification payloads. Keep logs independent of account existence where public data might be exposed. Failure paths render recoverable generic notices without claiming success or disclosing state. An in-memory diagnostic counter is optional; do not introduce external telemetry or transmission. For this demo, restart drops all state and reseeds synthetic accounts; there is **no migration** or persistent schema. If durable/multi-worker operation is later approved, design a separate migration, uniqueness/transaction strategy, shared session revocation, cross-worker rate limit, reliable notification outbox and operational secret management rather than treating this design as production-ready.

## Significant proposed decisions (alternatives and rationale)

| Decision | Alternative considered | Reason / limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flask app with server-side templates and thin route/service/store boundaries | JavaScript SPA, external API/microservices | Directly matches the Python 3.12/Flask/server-rendered story; minimal independent components for the small demo (`REQ-016`, `REQ-017`). |
| One process-local in-memory store and private sink, no schema migration now | SQLite/external DB, email/SMS provider | Fits synthetic/in-memory constraint and no deployment; sacrifices restart/multi-worker guarantees (`REQ-014`, `REQ-015`, `REQ-019`). |
| Sliding one-hour accepted-issuance window with generic outward acknowledgement for all valid identifiers, including capped ones | Public 429/status/text on capped known accounts; fixed hourly buckets | A known-only 429 would disclose account existence; bucket rollover could accept >5 in a trailing hour. Unknown-account rate accounting and response wording remain reviewer questions (`REQ-007`, `REQ-008`). |
| CSPRNG bearer token stored only as digest, checked at completion and consumed with password/session update | Predictable token or stateless signed link | Enables 30-minute issuance-based expiry, single use and atomic replay rejection (`REQ-009`–`REQ-011`). Raw link must exist transiently in the private sink, but not public confirmation. |
| Server-side opaque session registry and a reset-intent handoff | Pure signed-cookie authentication state or raw token posted in HTML | Allows invalidating all application-represented active sessions without disclosing the reset link in S4 markup. Does **not** assert a specified sign-in outcome; multiple-session creation may be tested via fixtures pending owner decision (`REQ-012`). |
| Owner notice appended after successful state changes in same logical unit of work | External send on request path; best-effort notice after returning success | Keeps every successful reset associated with a private owner notice and avoids false success after sink failure (`REQ-013`, `REQ-015`). External delivery is not available. |
| No deployment work and no deployment workflow | Container/hosting setup | Explicit story boundary; future hosting would require separate approval (`REQ-020`, `REQ-021`). |

## Coverage handoff and unresolved choices

All approved requirements remain implementation obligations, not completed work: S1 markup covers `REQ-001`, `REQ-002`, `REQ-003`, `REQ-004`, `REQ-005`; recovery entry `REQ-006`; uniform request and limit `REQ-007`, `REQ-008`; one-time/expiry/completion `REQ-009`, `REQ-010`, `REQ-011`; session invalidation and owner notice `REQ-012`, `REQ-013`; synthetic/in-memory boundary `REQ-014`, `REQ-015`; runtime and server rendering `REQ-016`, `REQ-017`; pytest `REQ-018`; production-limit documentation `REQ-019`; no deployment/workflows `REQ-020`, `REQ-021`. The later contract must give each ID one or more dependency-ordered `TASK-NNN` assignments or an explicit justified disposition; this T001 architecture draft creates neither implementation tasks nor a deliverable contract.

Open questions for subsequent design/review, not facts to infer: whether Sign in actually authenticates and how sessions originate outside test fixtures; whether the proposed uniform capped-request acknowledgement is desired and whether unknown-account abuse needs a separate non-disclosing control; owner access to a private sink link without external transport; minimum/confirmation password rules; exact recovery-screen routes, copy, accessibility focus/error conventions, and layout; whether restart persistence or multiple workers will ever be required. The present design intentionally assumes none of those additional capabilities are requirements.
